source: What Child Is This - We Voice (Part 1 of 2), Entry 1

blocks.text: 01: Is Christmas a historical event or a religious myth dressed up in historical clothing?

sentences: Every December, the Christmas story moves back into the center of public life and experience.
It shows up on greeting cards, in department store windows, and in the music piped through airports and train stations..
It is usually the central theme in church services that fill to capacity with people who haven't been there since last year.
To put it lightly, the story is simply everywhere.
The question that is almost never asked out loud, though plenty of people are asking it privately is, “Did any of it actually happen?”
Let’s stop right here and recognize the elephant in the room…
This isn't an unfair question.
In fact, it’s not just a good question.
It's the right one.
A story that fills two thousand years of human history, reshapes the calendar, and generates more discussion than any other event ever recorded in the Western world deserves more than just sentiment.
This question deserves an honest investigation.

So…let's start where any good Christmas investigation should start: not with the shepherds, not with magi, not with the manger, not with the angels, not with Mary, not with Joseph, not with Luke, and not with Matthew.
Let’s go back to the literal square one but with the person at the center of the story and ask the most foundational question possible.
Was Jesus of Nazareth a real human being who existed on the pages of history?
Because if He wasn't, Christmas is a myth.
Full stop.
We can appreciate it as literature, celebrate it as tradition, and enjoy it as a season, but we can't call it history.
If, on the other hand, Jesus of Nazareth was a real historical figure, then His birth isn't a myth.
It's a guaranteed historical fact.
A person who exists must have been born.
That isn't a theological argument.
It's a logical one.
Here is where the investigation leads first, and the results aren't what many people expect.
The historical existence of Jesus of Nazareth isn't a live debate among scholars.
It was settled long ago, and it wasn't settled by Christian scholars alone.

John Dominic Crossan, who spent decades leading the Jesus Seminar and whose skepticism about the gospels is well documented, wrote that the crucifixion of Jesus is as certain as anything in ancient history can be.

Bart Ehrman, an atheist and one of the most widely read New Testament scholars in the world, wrote that the idea Jesus never existed is a modern notion with no ancient precedent, invented in the eighteenth century.
Geza Vermes, a Jewish scholar, placed Jesus squarely in first-century Galilee as a figure who was baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate.
N.T. Wright, speaking from the Christian side, noted that the existence of Jesus of Nazareth is as well established as any fact from the ancient world.
These aren't fringe voices.
They represent the full spectrum of scholarly opinion: skeptic, atheist, Jewish, Christian.
When that entire spectrum reaches the same conclusion, we're not dealing with a matter of faith.
We're dealing with a matter of fact.
We might push back here and say that scholars are one thing, but primary sources are another.
That's a fair instinct.
So let's go to the primary sources.

Not to the Bible, which the skeptic will dismiss as interested testimony, but to the record of Rome, of first-century Jewish historians, and of the pagan critics who actively wanted to undermine the Christian movement.

blocks.text: THE WITNESSES WHO HAD NO REASON TO HELP

sentences: Cornelius Tacitus was a Roman senator and historian writing around AD 116.
He had every professional reason to be dismissive of a Jewish religious movement that his class considered a dangerous superstition.

In his Annals, in a passage about the great fire of Rome under Nero, Tacitus records that Christus, from whom the name Christians derived, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius, at the hands of Pontius Pilate.
He goes on to note that the movement was suppressed momentarily but broke out again and spread from Judea to Rome itself.
This is the single strongest extra-biblical witness to the historical Jesus.
Tacitus is hostile.
He has no motive to help the Christian cause.
What he provides isn't endorsement.
It's evidence.
Josephus was a first-century Jewish historian writing for a Roman audience.
He wasn't a Christian, and he wasn't friendly to Christian claims.
Yet in his Antiquities of the Jews, written around AD 93, he references Jesus twice.

The first passage, known as the Testimonium Flavianum, contains sections scholars widely believe were embellished by later Christian copyists, but the core reference to a teacher executed under Pilate is broadly accepted as original.
The second passage, which carries no textual controversy, references James as the brother of Jesus who was called Christ.
A Jewish historian who was hostile to the Jesus movement left two references to Him in his major work.
He couldn't ignore the figure because the figure was too historically significant to omit.
Pliny the Younger was a Roman governor who wrote to Emperor Trajan around AD 112 seeking advice on how to handle Christians in his province.
His letter isn't theology.
It's a government report describing a logistical problem.
He notes that Christians were gathering before dawn on a fixed day to sing hymns to Christ as to a god, and binding themselves by oath to live ethically.
He's reporting organized worship of Jesus as divine from the early second century.
The movement had grown visible enough to require imperial attention within eighty years of the crucifixion.
Celsus, a pagan philosopher writing around AD 175, produced the first known comprehensive intellectual assault on Christianity.
His work survives because the early Christian scholar Origen preserved it in order to answer it, which is itself a remarkable detail.
Christians kept their critic's strongest arguments.
What Celsus never argues, for all his hostility, is that Jesus didn't exist.
He argues instead that Jesus was born under scandalous circumstances, learned magic in Egypt, and deceived His followers.
Celsus disputes the meaning of Jesus.
He takes for granted the existence of the man.

Beyond these four, Suetonius, a Roman court historian writing around AD 120, references disturbances in Rome instigated by one named Chrestus, widely understood as a reference to Christ and the friction His movement was generating in the Roman Jewish community.
Lucian of Samosata, a Greek satirist, mocks Christians as devoted to a man who was crucified in Palestine.
Mara bar Serapion, a Syrian Stoic philosopher, refers to the execution of a wise Jewish king.
None of these men are friends of the gospel.
None of them have any motive to provide the historical record they provide.
Together with Tacitus, Josephus, and Pliny, they form an external witness array that any ancient historian would consider robust.

blocks.text: THE LOGIC THAT CLOSES THE QUESTION

sentences: Here is what all of this establishes, stated plainly.
Jesus of Nazareth was a real person who walked the actual ground of first-century Judea, gathered followers, taught publicly, and was executed by Roman authority under Pontius Pilate.
His existence is attested by Roman historians, a Jewish historian, a Roman provincial governor, and his own adversaries.
The historical record outside of Scripture alone is sufficient to place Him in history.
Once that's established, what follows isn't a leap.
It's a deduction.
A person who exists must have been born.
A historical figure with an attested life, a datable execution, and documented followers must have had a beginning.
The birth of Jesus isn't a separate question requiring a separate investigation.
It's the necessary implication of the answer we've already reached.
If Jesus lived, Jesus was born.
And if Jesus was born, Christmas isn't a myth.
It's, at minimum, a historical event.
Whether Christmas is anything more than a historical event, whether the birth in Bethlehem was also the arrival of God in human flesh, is a larger question.
That question will occupy the rest of this book.
We shouldn't skip to it before we've secured the ground beneath our feet.
The ground is secure.
The birth happened.
The story is real.
There's one more thing worth naming before we move on.
Someone may object that the Christmas story, with its angels and shepherds and a star that moves, sounds miraculous, and that miracles belong to the realm of religion rather than history.
That objection will get a full answer later in this book.
For now, one observation is enough.
The question of whether miracles happen is a separate question from the question of whether this particular story happened.
Every serious historian who has examined the life of Jesus, whether or not they believe in miracles, places Him in history.
The investigation doesn't end with the discovery that the story sounds miraculous.
It begins there.
Most of us came to our conclusions about Christmas without examining the historical evidence.
What would it mean to revisit those conclusions with the same tools we'd bring to any other historical question?
The scholars most quoted to deny the historicity of Jesus, including Bart Ehrman, are often the same scholars who confirm it most directly.
What does it tell us that the strongest case for the existence of Jesus comes partly from people who don't believe He was God?
Celsus attacked Christianity for decades without once arguing that Jesus never existed.
Why would it have served his purposes to skip that argument if the argument had been available to him?
The argument that Christmas is myth rather than history is, by the standard of ancient historical evidence, among the weakest positions a person can hold.
If we're willing to accept the existence of Julius Caesar, Augustus, or Tiberius on the basis of comparable evidence, on what grounds do we treat the evidence for Jesus differently?
If the birth of Jesus is a guaranteed implication of His historical existence, where does that leave the instinct to treat Christmas as merely symbolic or culturally traditional rather than factual?
